#### Executive Briefing
- **Nvidia** has instructed manufacturing partners to pause server [shipments to](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-88bbfb00194a) Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia as tightened US export controls aim to keep AI chips out of China. The pause is a material setback for Southeast Asia's data-center buildout and a sharp escalation in chip geopolitics.
- **Microsoft** published details on ARTEX, an AI framework that state-backed hackers have used since July 2026 [to automate cyberattacks](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-ab5ddf0b7ed2) through specialized agents with minimal human oversight, attributed to groups in China and North Korea plus criminal organizations. It is concrete evidence that offensive AI cyber capabilities are operational today, not theoretical.
- **Compute, data, and usage limits became battlegrounds**: OpenAI and Anthropic restricted data access, reportedly pushing Z.AI and Moonshot AI to delay flagship launches and turn [to Google and Meta](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-35150db404c8) for training data, while OpenAI cut GPT-6.2 allowances days after launch — Astra users now hit [limits 40](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-b7ac755e2890)% faster and Sol users 25% faster.
- **AI mathematics hit the mainstream**: former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson argued the recent AI-assisted Riemann proof matters less for its result than for [the fact that an AI system](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-89fce0273ad2) could produce it, warning labs may hold unpublished cryptographic advances. Separately, a researcher described [months of Astra-assisted work with a mathematics professor on long-standing open problems](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-e4b84d466755).

#### Safety & Regulation
- **England and Wales courts**: an investigation found at least 25 cases in 2026 were [affected by undisclosed AI use](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-a2b781a0780b), including AI-generated witness statements, fabricated case law, and nonexistent statutes, prompting judicial complaints — quantified evidence that undisclosed AI is already straining legal safeguards.
- **OpenAI** confirmed that Private Inference, a confidential-computing capability keeping [prompts and responses](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-ecdab81b4811) under strict control even during model processing, is now in testing. It targets the confidentiality concerns that keep banks, health systems, and other regulated industries off frontier APIs.

#### Research Highlights
- **DexEngine** is a simulation pipeline that converts everyday human hand-object video [into physically executable whole-robot](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) arm-hand trajectories using reachability-aware placement, motion retargeting, and residual RL correction, producing roughly 65,000 trajectories and 325,000 episodes across nine datasets. It attacks dexterous manipulation's central data bottleneck, promising far cheaper training of capable robot policies.
- **NOPO ([Negative-Only Policy Optimization](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-d4361145e47d))** formalizes one-sided verifiable rewards — where confirmed negatives are trustworthy but "positives" are merely non-falsified — and trains policies only by suppressing trusted negatives. This matches realistic verifiers in code, math, and agent settings, cutting reward-hacking risk where positive verification is unreliable.
- **"[Speak When You See It](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-2fce1ed16bca)"** shows two proactive-assistant benchmarks can be dominated by a video-blind timer policy that ignores video content entirely, formalizing a "video-blind frontier" and proposing an evidence-based decision framework instead. The lesson is that flawed benchmarks can silently reward shortcuts and misdirect assistant research.

#### Trending Repositories
- **[cathrynlavery/diagram-design](/?date=2026-11-27&category=github_trending#item-1cbbd89c355a)** (731 stars today) generates editorial-quality diagrams across 52 types as self-contained HTML and SVG, working inside Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, and other coding agents. Developers are adopting it to fix the chronically weak visual output of coding assistants.
- **[zhouxiaoka/autoclip](/?date=2026-11-27&category=github_trending#item-6e8f56a7cafa)** (733 stars today) is a local-first, open-source alternative to OpusClip that turns one link into a finished clip with zero subscriptions, including an MCP server for agent workflows — part of rising demand for subscription-free, locally run AI media tools.
- **[HKUDS/CLI-Anything](/?date=2026-11-27&category=github_trending#item-02fa09d11035)** (668 stars today) aims to make all software agent-native so coding agents can operate everyday command-line tools directly, extending today's clear pattern of developers rewarding agent-infrastructure projects that remove concrete workflow bottlenecks.

#### Signals to Watch
- **The open-source-versus-proprietary fight escalated**: Yann LeCun accused proprietary labs like OpenAI and Anthropic of being "[black holes](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-afe4276bf491)" that absorb open research without contributing back, while Timnit Gebru called anti-open-source criticism corporate propaganda protecting a few [US companies](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-9acbf058f5cd) — a clash that will shape coming policy battles over open weights.
- **Verifiability remains contested**: OpenAI's Jason Wei argued [verifiability is a](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-83d1841b700b) spectrum, claiming even "non-verifiable" tasks can be judged by experts or market signals, just as papers like NOPO and the video-blind benchmark study push the field toward stricter, more honest evaluation.
- **Agents are spreading into go-to-market work**: [Clay](/?date=2026-11-27&category=news#item-99e4aaef9af6), a GTM automation platform that raised $115M at a $7.1B valuation in September, reports roughly half of its usage now runs through external harnesses like Claude Code, signaling agent workflows are moving beyond coding into sales and revenue operations.

top_items.title: How Clay Builds GTM Agents — Jeff Barg, Head of AI
top_items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use.  Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation.  By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph.  Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings.  The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows.  Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion →Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks.  Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion →$1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market.  Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion →Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company.  The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion →No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work.  Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion →Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected.  The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion →Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did.  When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion →Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand.  Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. Jump to the agent debugging discussion →Show notesClay — the go-to-market platform where Jeff is Head of AI. Clay raises $115M to be the AI growth engine for every company — the September Series D at a $7.1 billion valuation, led by Wellington. Clay acquires Avenue to help growth teams act on intent signals — the January 2025 deal that brought Jeff's team to Clay. How Clay Scales GTM Agents — Jeff's LangChain Interrupt talk on running Clay's agents in production. Clay Agent Plugin (CLI & API) — the CLI and API that let Claude Code and Codex work directly with Clay. Inside Clay Workflows — how Workflows was built, including the table view customers asked to get back. Sellers have a new AI edge: Clay in ChatGPT — the ChatGPT app launch from Jeff's story. Sculpt recap: Building the self-learning revenue engine — Clay's October launches, including its new agent and Workflows. TypeSafe launched Jev because sequential LLMs are "totally useless for computers" — The New Stack on the classifier model behind Jeff's $1,500 math. top_items.content_html: Open video on YouTube ↗Clay wants you to get about the same results whether you use its own agent or point Claude Code at Clay. Usage is already split close to 50/50 between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses. In this episode, we chat with Jeff Barg, Head of AI at Clay, about what it takes to build go-to-market infrastructure that any agent can use. Jeff joined Clay when it acquired Avenue, the ops alerting startup he cofounded. At the time, Clay had about 50 people, and Avenue had five. AI was already a big part of how Clay thought about its product, but nobody there worked on AI. Since then, the business has grown roughly 10x, and the team is up to around 600 people. In September, Clay raised $115 million at a $7.1 billion valuation. By Jeff’s napkin math, it would cost about $1,500 to check all 40 million companies in Clay’s database against your ideal customer profile with a classifier like TypeSafe’s Jev. Models have been acing Clay’s lead-qualification evals for about a year now. Jeff sees more value in using frontier models for orchestration and deep research. We also talk about why customers hate picking a model, how Clay plans to pick one for them, and why the team still runs its agents on a system it built with BullMQ, without Temporal or LangGraph. Jeff tells us what happened when OpenAI called off Clay’s ChatGPT apps launch with two days to go. We get into why customers hated Workflows at first, how agents came to build most workflows, and when post-training pays off. We also talk about why agents still can’t debug other agents, even as Clay’s agent can count its YC customers in about a minute. Sculptor started as a tool loop. Now it's a coding agent. When Jeff took over as Head of AI, one engineer was doing all of Clay’s agent work. He soon left to start his own company. Claude Code changed what Jeff wanted to build. His first launch was Sculptor, which shipped in September 2025 on models from the Sonnet 3.5 era. It ran a set of tools in a loop with a system prompt the team had spent a lot of time tuning. It was great at adding columns but terrible at booking ten qualified meetings. The evals didn’t catch much. Clay used an LLM to judge which tools Sculptor called. That missed things people actually did with it, like asking it to analyze a table or giving it an enterprise table with millions of rows. Jeff took away three lessons. Coding agents are really good at Bash and Python. Sculptor’s tools were too limited to do much by stringing them together. And the agent couldn’t see CRM data or campaign results. So Clay rebuilt Sculptor as a coding agent on the Pi harness. It runs the Clay CLI in a cloud sandbox. A new data layer called Audiences matches records across the CRM and Gong so the agent can see them together. Jump to the Sculptor discussion →Most companies post-train too early For Jeff’s first eighteen months at Clay, the team talked about training its own models. It only started to look viable in the past couple of months. Jeff sees two ways to bring costs down. First, swap in an off-the-shelf open-weight model, which is already much cheaper than Opus. Then you can post-train a smaller model on your own tools and queries until it does as well as Opus on your tasks. Jeff sees companies make two mistakes here. One is trying to beat the frontier models, which is still really hard even in a single domain. The other is starting before you spend enough on inference for the savings to matter. Jeff puts that threshold somewhere between $10 million and $100 million. Jump to the post-training discussion →$1,500 to score every company in the world Clay hasn’t put TypeSafe’s Jev into production yet, but Jeff has run the numbers. Clay’s database has about 40 million companies. A LinkedIn page is roughly a thousand tokens, and an ideal customer profile adds about 500 more. Ask a classifier whether each company is a good fit, and the bill for all 40 million comes to around $1,500. Today, most customers qualify a list of maybe 10,000 companies. At these prices, you can start with the entire market. Jeff puts a good enrichment budget at $1 to $10 per qualified lead and $10 to $100 per booked call. He thinks qualification itself is close to solved. Models have been scoring about as high as they can on Clay’s evals for roughly a year. Just about any model from the past year can pull a company’s latest funding round. Frontier models still matter for deep prospecting research and for orchestration, where Jeff says the best plays can be ten to a hundred times as effective as an average one. Jump to the Jev discussion →Customers hate the model selector Customers complain when they see Clay’s model selector. They can’t check the evals for their use case every time a new model ships, and they shouldn’t have to. Clay is about to launch an automatic router that picks a model for each task. There’s no fancy branding. Finding Apple’s CEO is a very different job from finding the CEO of an obscure local company. The selector isn’t going away. Agency owners and power users still want control. Everyone else just wants to get on with their work. Clay has to earn their trust before they’ll leave it on auto. Jump to the model routing discussion →No Temporal, no LangGraph Clay built most of its agent stack itself. It uses BullMQ to keep agent jobs running, Postgres and ClickHouse for product data, and Snowflake for analytics. Jeff isn’t sure how BullMQ will hold up if usage grows another tenfold, but it’s held up so far. Clay recently shipped 25 to 30 new integrations. Contracts and testing took longer than the engineering work. Where Clay did run into trouble was scale. People run an agent per row, so if someone starts a run on a table of 50,000 companies, inference demand spikes all at once. Clay brought in LangSmith to see what was happening. The team also built a way to throttle requests and to pause and resume work when a provider goes down or starts rate-limiting. The harder part is keeping things fair. Someone running a workflow for ten people still needs it to run when an enterprise customer is enriching a million rows. Jump to the infrastructure discussion →Built for every agent, not just Clay's Clay plans to ship a sandboxed agent that’s free to use any of Clay’s tools and building blocks. Jeff wants someone using Clay from Claude Code to get about the same results. People should be able to use Clay wherever they already work. Usage is already much closer to a 50/50 split between Clay’s agent and outside harnesses than Jeff expected. The push came from inside Clay. Its own go-to-market team lived in Cursor and wouldn’t leave it, so they asked for a CLI. The MCP team switched over to build it, and Clay’s sales team now does deal prep in Codex. So why build a first-party agent at all? Plenty of customers live in the Clay UI and want an agent right there. Jump to the agent platform discussion →Keep building when the plan blows up Jeff thinks it takes more courage to change plans at 600 people than it did at 50. Clay was a launch partner for ChatGPT apps. In the middle of the quarter, Clay put about a quarter of its engineers on the integration for a month. Two days before launch, OpenAI postponed it indefinitely. Clay kept building on the assumption that OpenAI would change its mind. Three or four days later, it did. When Clay first showed customers Workflows, they were confused. Some were upset. They wanted their spreadsheet. Now agency owners like it, and a growing share of the work that used to run in tables runs in Workflows. Most workflows are built with the CLI or the agent. CEO Kareem Amin spent five years building Clay when almost nothing was working. Jeff still sees that persistence in the company today. Jump to the ChatGPT apps discussion →Agents still can't debug agents What Jeff wants most is a model that can read a long agent trace and tell him where the run went wrong. Today’s models tend to flag whichever step took a long time, even when the mistake was somewhere else. Clay would like to pull traces from bad runs, have an agent review them and use what it finds to improve the agent automatically. That still doesn’t work, and Clay writes a lot of its skills by hand. Models still make basic mistakes, like retrying the same CLI command with the same inputs over and over. But when Jeff wanted to know how many YC companies use Clay, he asked the agent and had the answer in about a minute. A year ago, he would’ve had to scrape the batch, get access to Snowflake and cross-reference the two by hand. top_items.title: Your future housekeeper might be an XPeng
top_items.content: Your future housekeeper might be an XPeng PLUS: Amazon drone crashes trigger FAA scrutiny Jennifer Mossalgue , Rowan Cheung , Shubham Sharma & Zach Mink November 26, 2026 Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, robotics enthusiasts. China’s XPeng has unveiled an upgraded IRON humanoid that could greet car buyers by early 2027 — and tackle household chores a year or two after that. The move intensifies a race against Tesla, Figure AI, and a growing field of Chinese robotics companies looking to turn impressive humanoid demos into commercially useful machines, with the home robot as the ultimate prize. The details: IRON packs 76 degrees of freedom, 1,500+ tactile sensing points, and three Turing AI chips, with autonomous navigation and self-charging capabilities. XPeng targets mass production in January 2027, retail-assistant training in Q1, and a public release in Q2. Co-president Brian Gu told CNBC that home deployment could follow successful commercial use by one to two years, though no firm timeline has been set. XPeng is using the same AI architecture, VLA 3.0, to power both its humanoids and self-driving vehicles, including its YOYO-01 robotaxi, slated for 2027. Why it matters: XPeng is building IRON on the AI and data pipeline developed for its cars, but it’s chasing AgiBot and Unitree, which shipped ~16.7K humanoids in the first half of 2026. Homes also pose a tougher challenge than showrooms, with people often changing interiors and kids and pets running around. AMAZON 📦 FAA probes Amazon’s Michigan drone crash Image source: Amazon The Rundown: The FAA is reportedly investigating Amazon after a Prime Air drone dropped off a bottle of shampoo in a Detroit suburb, caught a fiber line on the way out, and ended up jammed against a neighbor’s garage roof. The details: Amazon’s MK30 drone reportedly hit a fiber-optic line on the climb, lost a propeller, and landed between a garage roof and an electrical cable. Amazon says the drone uses cameras and sensors to identify hazards, including power lines, and adjusts its flight when it detects an obstruction. The FAA is weighing corrective or enforcement action; the NTSB hasn’t decided whether to open a case. Waco, Texas, logged a similar strike last year, when an MK30 hit an internet line after a delivery and drew an FAA investigation. Why it matters: Amazon says Prime Air has delivered hundreds of thousands of packages in 2026, with nearly 6K flights daily. Still, similar collisions involving wires in Texas, a crane in Arizona, and an apartment building raise questions about how reliably its drones can navigate obstacles as deliveries scale up. NANOBOTS 🧠 Light-powered nanobots carry chemo into brains Image source: Gao Lab / Caltech The Rundown: Caltech researchers just said their light-activated BrainBots delivered about five times as much chemotherapy to mouse brains as unactivated carriers, potentially offering a new approach to getting drugs past the brain’s defenses. The details: Near-infrared light propels the 250nm carriers, as attached DNA molecules help them bind to cells that transport them across the blood–brain barrier. Eight hours after dosing, activated BrainBots delivered 5.2x as much doxorubicin to brain tissue as unactivated carriers, according to the researchers. In mice with glioblastoma, treatment slowed tumor growth and extended survival while reducing systemic toxicity compared with conventional methods. Oxford neuroscientist Tim Viney told the Financial Times that the tissue and neuroanatomical evidence needed “significant improvement” and questioned whether the approach could translate to humans. Why it matters: BrainBots join a growing field of experimental brain-delivery systems, including “ Trojanbots ” that use immune cells to carry chemotherapy-loaded nanobots toward brain tumors in mice. Another approach has already reached human trials: ultrasound and injected microbubbles to open the blood-brain barrier during chemo. ZOOX 🔊 Zoox tests gentler robotaxi warnings Image source: Zoox The Rundown: Zoox is building a street vocabulary for its robotaxis, starting with a better way to say “watch out.” In tests with Virginia Tech, custom warning tones warned would-be jaywalkers as reliably as a honking horn, without the jarring noise. The details: Forty participants, including 20 with low vision or visual impairments, completed 360 crossing trials: 200 midblock and 160 at marked crosswalks. The research vehicles featured

### Executive Signal
- Today's strongest research concentrates on three fronts: [scaling](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) robot learning data from human video, making reinforcement learning honest when verifiers can only reliably reject wrong answers, and tightening evaluation methodology. Benchmarks that silently reward shortcut policies, plus new pipelines for dexterous manipulation and streaming video efficiency, signal a field prioritizing rigor and deployability.

### Priority Developments
- **DexEngine** converts everyday human hand-object video [into physically executable whole-robot](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) arm-hand trajectories through a reachability-aware simulation pipeline. Because dexterous manipulation data is the field's central bottleneck, a scalable human-to-robot pipeline could sharply cut the cost of training capable robot policies.
- **NOPO ([Negative-Only Policy Optimization](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-d4361145e47d))** formalizes one-sided verifiable rewards, where verified negatives are reliable but positives are merely non-falsified, and trains purely from confirmed negatives. This matches realistic verifier regimes in code, math, and agent settings, making RLVR more trustworthy in deployed pipelines.
- **AIChipBench** tasks LLM coding agents with implementing synthesizable RTL decoders for quantized **Qwen3.5**, **Gemma 3**, **Gemma 4**, and **Llama 3.2**, validated bit-level against reference hardware. Automated [accelerator design](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-421d0b03bc10) is economically significant, and this benchmark quantifies how far current agents remain from reliable hardware generation.
- **LiveVAE** shows pretrained video VAEs depend almost entirely on local spatiotemporal neighborhoods, then exploits this with [causal window attention](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-b7791b8110c4) to build an efficient streaming VAE. Reduced latency and cost for video processing directly benefits real-time generation, world models, and streaming applications.
- **[Speak When You See It](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-2fce1ed16bca)** proves two proactive-assistant benchmarks can be dominated by a video-blind timer policy that ignores video content entirely, formalizing this as a 'video-blind frontier.' Benchmark integrity matters because flawed evaluation can misdirect progress on proactive assistants.

### Leadership Implications
- Audit verifier reliability before scaling RL post-training: **NOPO** and the text-to-SQL reward-hacking study show that weak verification, including partial [single-database](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-79a8205f3b94) checks, can silently corrupt training. Build reward-hacking diagnostics into standard practice.
- Robotics and agent teams should track data-scaling pipelines (**DexEngine**) and self-improvement loops (**[RoboEvo](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-c5c439745b78)^2**, **ELITE**) as emerging alternatives to costly [human demonstrations](/?date=2026-11-27&category=research#item-58ae6b113fef) and evaluation-heavy iteration. These results suggest cheaper, more autonomous training cycles are becoming practical.

top_items.title: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data
top_items.content: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.

top_items.title: Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
top_items.content: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically relies on a verifier that can reliably judge whether sampled solutions are correct. However, in many realistic settings, complete verification is generally unavailable, while cheap checks can only falsify failures. We formalize this regime as one-sided verifiability (OSV): verified negatives are reliable counterexamples, but verified positives are merely non-falsified candidates and may contain many false positives. This asymmetry makes standard RLVR unreliable, because reinforcing verified positives can directly reward shortcuts that pass partial checks. To address this issue, we propose Negative-Only Policy Optimization (NOPO), which treats verified positives as unlabeled and updates the policy only by suppressing trusted verified negatives. Specifically, NOPO combines a reference-relative negative suppression loss with a group-level adapter that scales each update by the proportion of non-falsified responses. Across unit-test, constraint-check, and LLM self-verifiers, NOPO improves pass@k over baselines on code, logic, and math benchmarks when oracle rewards are unavailable. These gains persist under inference-time scaling and cross-benchmark transfer.

top_items.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
top_items.content: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

top_items.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
top_items.content: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.

top_items.title: EgoUseBench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents under Evolving First-Person Contexts
top_items.content: AI wearables, such as smart glasses, extend the context available to agents beyond digital environments to users' physical surroundings. With these devices, computer tasks can originate from users' ongoing activities rather than solely from explicit instructions. Through first-person observations, agents can identify objects and activities relevant to user requests and ground digital tasks in the surrounding context. We call this interaction paradigm Ego Use. However, first-person observations are limited by the wearer's viewpoint and may provide incomplete or ambiguous evidence of ongoing activities. As new observations arrive, agents may need to revise their understanding of the physical context and user intent, and reassess whether prior digital actions remain valid. Whether current agents can reliably handle these changes remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce EgoUseBench, a benchmark for evaluating Ego Use across three interaction settings with different levels of first-person context. Computer-Use relies on explicit instructions, Offline Ego Use provides prerecorded first-person context before execution, and Online Ego Use provides continuous observations as user intent evolves. Based on over 74 hours of real-world first-person recordings, we construct 693 tasks across the three interaction settings. To capture task evolution, we track first-person observations, user requirements, and website state separately. We further group tasks by how information changes during execution, resulting in three types: Graft (revised user requirements), Refresh (new first-person observations), and Clarify (agent-initiated information seeking). We evaluate advanced models and find that average success rates in Online Ego Use are 26.3% lower than in Computer-Use. This result reveals the difficulty of keeping task execution aligned with evolving first-person context and user intent.

- The dominant debate today is **open-source versus [proprietary AI](/?date=2026-11-27&category=social#item-afe4276bf491)**: **Yann LeCun** accuses closed labs of absorbing open research without contributing back, while **Timnit Gebru** calls anti-open-source criticism corporate propaganda. Dodds**' temporary-verification-test pattern offers a practical template for keeping agentic codebases maintainable.

top_items.content:
Imagine a robot walking in a museum and mapping everything it sees.

The robot uses every camera frame to estimate where it is and build a 3D representation.

But generating a good map is hard: every small error can accumulate as the robot moves, causing the map to gradually drift out of alignment.

@robbyant_brain addresses this with LingBot-Map 2.0:

It's a model that takes video and estimates the camera's path and the scene's 3D geometry frame by frame.

This version has a new feature: Refine, and the way it works is pretty cool:

• Refine updates the geometric context the model uses to estimate the camera trajectory.

• It saves those updates to the model so it can improve existing reconstructions and use the updated geometry to process future frames.

• You can trigger Refine at any point during a run to reduce accumulated drift.

And all of this happens inside the model, without any external optimization backend.

Look at the attached demo:

• The orange path is the estimated camera trajectory before Refine.
• The cyan path shows the corrected trajectory after Refine.

This is one of the key capabilities supporting the embodied-native, general-purpose robot brain @robbyant_brain is building. Without reliable spatial memory, autonomous work over large areas and long hours isn't possible.

Here is more information about the model:

• Project page: https://technology.robbyant.com/lingbot-map-v2

• Technical report: https://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-map-v2/blob/main/docs/lingbot-map-v2_paper.pdf

• GitHub: https://github.com/Robbyant/lingbot-map-v2

• Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/robbyant/lingbot-map-v2

The Streaming version is open source; Refine is not included.
